title: Writing Tests
concept: Test functions annotated with `@test` are discovered and executed by the test runner
why: Tests are code that verifies other code. Writing tests forces you to think about edge cases, expected behavior, and failure modes before shipping. Each test is a small, focused assertion: 'given this input, I expect this output.' Tests also serve as executable documentation — they show how your API is meant to be used.
theory: A test in XIOM is a function with the `@test` attribute that takes no parameters and returns nothing. The test runner compiles all `@test` functions into a test binary, calls each one, and reports pass/fail. A test passes if it runs without panicking; a test fails if an assertion fails or the function panics. Tests can live in the same file as the code (inline tests) or in dedicated test modules. The `@test` attribute supports an optional name: `@test("descriptive name")`.
tips: Follow the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern in every test
Test both positive cases (expected input) and negative cases (edge cases)
Name tests descriptively — `test_empty_input_returns_none` is better than `test1`
common_mistakes: Writing tests that don't assert anything (they always pass)
Testing too many things in one test function
Using real network/filesystem in unit tests instead of mocking
